newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian foreign minister delays Cambodia visit.
newsitem.headline: Australian foreign minister delays Cambodia visit.

text.p: Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer on Friday delayed a planned visit to Cambodia to avoid indicating support for the new regime of Hun Sen, who seized power in a military takeover earlier this month.
"We didn't want any visit now to be seen as an endorsment of Hun Sen or his actions," a spokesman for Downer told Reuters.

The decision to delay the planned August 2-4 visit further increases pressure on Hun Sen, second prime minister in the ruling coalition government, to restore consitutional rule after ousting First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh in a widely condemned military takeover.
Australia's cabinet on Tuesday suspended Canberra's A$2 million (US$1.47 million) a year military aid programme in protest at Hun Sen's power grab.
But Canberra left in place its A$32 million civil aid package to the impoverished country, citing humanitarian reasons, subject to further review.

Stressing the visit would go ahead at a later date, Downer's spokesman said the original schedule did not allow time to determine the direction of the new regime in Phnom Penh or for it to develop policies.
Australia officially recognises states, not particular administrations, so formal recognition of the new administration is not an issue.

But Downer has said Canberra's Cambodia policy and relations with Phnom Penh would be determined by Cambodia's attitude to 1991 peace accords, the holding of free elections, and the inclusion in government of Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party.
Australian ambassador to Cambodia Tony Kevin, in a leaked diplomatic cable, has urged Canberra to back Hun Sen, describing the former power-sharing arrangement as sterile and unworkable.

According to a weekend newspaper report citing the cable, Kevin said Hun Sen remained a democrat at heart and was seeking to restore stable government. He also said Hun Sen could be pressed to honour his commitment to free and fair elections if the right kind of pressure was applied.

Downer said earlier this week he had received assurances on these issues from his Cambodian counterpart, Ung Huot, through Phnom Penh's ambassador to Australia, Vun Chheang. Ung Huot, a Royalist ally of the ousted Ranariddh, returned to Phnom Penh on Monday.
Ung Huot has since been named to replace Ranariddh as first prime minister and head of Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party.

Hun Sen, head of the Cambodian People's Party, and Ranariddh formed their power-sharing coalition after U.N.-organised elections in May 1993 which Ranariddh won. Never a happy alliance, the coalition began falling apart last year when Ranariddh demanded more power in the provinces.
